notes.reason: Scott writes the sentence himself, as a parenthetical that supports his argument: "no country outside the liberal mainstream has ever managed to equal current US happiness levels. The closest near-misses are Singapore at 6.5, and Saudi Arabia at 6.6." His two numbers are the World Happiness Report 2025 scores (Singapore 6.565, Saudi Arabia 6.600), and in that same 2025 table the United Arab Emirates scores 6.759 against the United States at 6.724, so a Gulf monarchy was already above the US in the dataset he was reading; Kuwait (6.629) was also closer than Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait beat the US outright in the 2024 report (6.95 against 6.725). The 2026 report, published four months before the post, puts the UAE at 6.821 and Saudi Arabia at 6.817 against the US at 6.816, and the mappr, Saudi Gazette and Arab News quotes the note rests on match those figures. I checked the numbers independently of the note's sources and they hold up. The claim matters to the argument, because the parenthetical is there to tell the reader that illiberal countries never reach liberal happiness levels, and Scott himself counts Saudi Arabia as outside the liberal mainstream, so the UAE plainly is too. The first reviewer's reservation, that the 2026 gaps are a few thousandths of a point, is not disqualifying: the note only says these countries "ranked above" the US, which is literally true, the 2025 UAE gap and the 2024 Kuwait gap are not tiny, and Scott's own word was "equal", which the 2026 scores satisfy on any reading. Scott may answer that oil-rich Gulf states are a special case, but that is a rejoinder, not a defence of the sentence as written, and he corrects factual slips like this readily.
